title: A Voice Memo About the Man Who Hides His Charity
script: Narrator: [reflective] There is an old man in my neighborhood named Pak Salim, and for years, strange good things kept happening to one particular family.
Narrator: [curious] Every Friday morning, an envelope of money appeared under their door, and nobody could ever explain who left it there.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Neighbors guessed and gossiped about it for months, but the mystery never really had an answer.
Narrator: [with wonder] Then one dawn, walking home early from the mosque, I saw Pak Salim slip something under that same door and walk away quickly.
Narrator: [surprised] I called his name softly, and he froze for a second, like a child caught doing something he shouldn't.
Narrator: [gently] I asked him directly, why do you hide this? Why not just knock and hand it to them yourself?
Narrator: [warmly] He looked at me for a long moment before answering, and his voice stayed calm and quiet the whole time.
Narrator: [sincere] He said, if I hand it to them myself, some part of me will want their thanks, even without meaning to.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He explained that a small hunger for praise can quietly ruin a good deed, even one done for the right reason at first.
Narrator: [warmly] He told me he had done this every single Friday for six years, and only Allah knew about it until that morning.
Narrator: [peacefully] He smiled and said the opposite was true. Not being seen made the act feel lighter, purer, more honest somehow.
Narrator: [reflective] He asked me to keep his secret, and I promised I would, though I am telling this story now without using his real name.
Narrator: [honestly] I realized I often wanted people to know when I helped someone, even quietly hoping the story would travel back to me.
Narrator: [determined] So I started something new. Once a month, I try to do one good thing that nobody will ever trace back to me.
Narrator: [gently] Sometimes it is a little money left somewhere quiet. Sometimes it is simply praying for someone who will never know I prayed for them.
Narrator: [peacefully] True sincerity, I now believe, means doing good even when no eyes are watching, not even our own need for recognition.

quiz.explanation: Every Friday morning, an envelope of money appeared under the family's door.

options: He saw him slip something under the door one dawn
quiz.explanation: Walking home early from the mosque, the narrator saw Pak Salim slip something under the door.

options: Part of him would want their thanks, even without meaning to
quiz.explanation: He explained that if he handed it over himself, part of him would want their thanks.

quiz.explanation: He said he had done this every Friday for six years before the narrator discovered it.

options: Telling everyone about his good deeds
Doing one untraceable good deed each month
Only helping people who thank him
quiz.explanation: He started doing one good thing each month that nobody could ever trace back to him.

title: A Nightly Phone Call to an Aging Mother
script: Mother: [warmly] Ridwan, you called again today. You called yesterday too, and the day before that.
Ridwan: [gently] I know, Ibu. I just like hearing your voice before I sleep.
Mother: [curious] You must be so busy with work. Don't your coworkers think it's strange, calling your mother every night?
Ridwan: [smiling] Some do, honestly. One asked me last week why I don't just call once a week like everyone else.
Mother: [gently] And what did you tell him?
Ridwan: [sincere] I told him I'm not doing this for him to understand, or for anyone to see. I do it for you, and for Allah.
Mother: [touched] That means more to me than you probably realize, my son.
Ridwan: [thoughtful] After Father passed away, I promised myself I would never let you feel forgotten, even on ordinary, boring days.
Mother: [softly] Some nights we barely talk about anything important. Just the weather, or what I cooked for dinner.
Ridwan: [warmly] Those small conversations are exactly what I want, Ibu. Nothing has to feel important for it to actually matter.
Mother: [reflective] Your brother calls once a month, and I love him deeply too, but something about your habit feels different.
Ridwan: [gently] I don't say this to compare myself to him. Everyone shows love in their own way, at their own pace.
Mother: [curious] Still, doesn't it get tiring, calling every single night without ever missing one?
Ridwan: [honestly] Some nights I am exhausted, and I almost skip it. But then I picture you waiting quietly by the phone.
Mother: [with love] I don't wait anxiously, but yes, I do notice, and I do feel it deeply when you call.
Ridwan: [sincere] That's exactly why I keep doing it, even when nobody at work knows how many nights this has already been.
Mother: [peacefully] You've never once mentioned this habit to your friends, have you?
Ridwan: [humbly] No, Ibu. It isn't something I want credit for. I just want you to feel loved quietly, every single day.
Mother: [warmly] Then you have already succeeded, my son, more than you could ever know.
Ridwan: [gently] Goodnight, Ibu. Sleep well. I'll call again tomorrow, like always.

quiz.question: How often does Ridwan call his mother?
quiz.explanation: The mother notes that Ridwan called again today, yesterday, and the day before that.

quiz.question: What did Ridwan tell his coworker who questioned the habit?
options: That he does it for her, and for Allah, not for others to see
That he has nothing else to do

quiz.explanation: Ridwan said he isn't doing it for anyone to understand or see, but for his mother and for Allah.

quiz.question: Why did Ridwan start calling every night?
options: He promised himself she would never feel forgotten after his father passed away
quiz.explanation: After his father passed away, he promised himself he would never let his mother feel forgotten.

quiz.question: What keeps Ridwan calling even on exhausted nights?
options: The thought of his mother waiting quietly by the phone
quiz.explanation: On tired nights, he pictures his mother waiting quietly by the phone and calls anyway.

options: Yes, he talks about it often
No, he has never mentioned it to them
quiz.explanation: Ridwan says he has never once mentioned this habit to his friends, because he doesn't want credit for it.

title: Praying Alone in the Dark
script: Narrator: [tired] Last night, I woke up alone at three in the morning, and the whole house was completely silent.
Narrator: [nervously] My body felt heavy, and part of me wanted to simply close my eyes and sleep again.
Narrator: [thoughtful] But I remembered something my grandmother always told me when I was still a young girl.
Narrator: [gently] She said, the sweetest prayers happen quietly, when nobody else is even awake to witness them.
Narrator: [determined] So I got up slowly, washed my face with cold water, and prayed quietly in the dark room.
Narrator: [calm] No one saw me. No one knew. It was just me, the darkness, and one small, honest moment.
Narrator: [reflective] I did not turn on a single light. I did not want the moment to feel prepared or performed in any way.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Somewhere in the middle of that prayer, I stopped thinking about being tired, and I simply felt present.
Narrator: [honestly] I have prayed in front of others many times, at the mosque, at family gatherings, in crowded rooms.
Narrator: [gently] Those prayers matter too, of course, but something about this one felt different, more mine somehow.
Narrator: [with wonder] Afterward, I felt a strange, gentle peace that stayed with me for the rest of the morning.
Narrator: [reflective] Nobody complimented me for waking up. Nobody even knew it happened, and that was exactly the point.
Narrator: [peacefully] I learned that private devotion often feels more real than anything ever done for others to witness or admire.
Narrator: [warmly] Now, some nights, I set an early alarm on purpose, just to sit quietly with Allah while the world sleeps.
Narrator: [sincere] Nobody applauds these quiet nights. No one ever will. And somehow, that has become exactly why I love them.

quiz.question: What time did the narrator wake up?
quiz.explanation: The narrator says she woke up alone at three in the morning.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandmother say about prayer?
options: Sleep is more important than prayer
The sweetest prayers happen quietly, when nobody else is awake to witness them
Prayer should always be shown to others
Mornings are the only good time to pray
quiz.explanation: Her grandmother said the sweetest prayers happen quietly, when nobody else is awake to witness them.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator not turn on the light?
options: She did not want the moment to feel prepared or performed
She could not find the switch
quiz.explanation: She says she did not turn on a light because she did not want it to feel prepared or performed.

quiz.question: How did this private prayer feel compared to praying in front of others?
quiz.explanation: She says this prayer felt different from praying with others, more hers somehow.

quiz.question: What does the narrator now sometimes do on purpose?
options: Set an early alarm to sit quietly with Allah while the world sleeps
quiz.explanation: She now sets an early alarm on purpose to sit quietly with Allah while the world sleeps.

title: A Podcast on What Sincerity Really Means
script: Host: [warmly] Welcome back to the show. Today my guest is Ilham, who wants to talk about sincerity, or ikhlas. Thanks for joining me.
Guest: [pleasantly] Thank you for having me. This topic changed my life a few years ago, so I'm glad to talk about it.
Host: [curious] For listeners who are unfamiliar, how would you explain sincerity in simple words?
Guest: [thoughtful] I would say sincerity means doing something good for Allah's sake alone, not for praise, not for image, not even for a good feeling.
Host: [interested] That sounds difficult to actually live out. Was there a moment that taught you this?
Guest: [reflective] Yes. A few years ago, I used to post about every good deed I did online, without even noticing the habit.
Host: [curious] What made you notice it?
Guest: [honestly] One day, I helped an elderly neighbor carry groceries, and my very first thought was, I should post this.
Host: [surprised] That's a very honest thing to admit.
Guest: [gently] It embarrassed me, actually. I realized the deed had quietly become about me, not about helping her.
Host: [curious] So what did you change after that?
Guest: [warmly] I started doing small good things and deliberately telling no one, not even my closest friends.
Host: [interested] Was that hard at first?
Guest: [honestly] Extremely hard. I kept wanting to mention it, almost out of habit, like an itch I had to scratch.
Host: [curious] Does it feel easier now?
Guest: [reflective] A little. But honestly, I think this is a lifelong practice, not something you finish and master completely.
Host: [thoughtful] What would you tell someone who struggles with wanting recognition for good deeds?
Guest: [encouraging] I would say, notice the urge without judging yourself too harshly, and gently choose quiet instead, again and again.
Host: [smiling] That's a beautiful, honest note to end on, Ilham. Thank you for sharing your story with us today.
Guest: [warmly] Thank you for listening. I hope it helps someone notice their own quiet urge for recognition too.

quiz.question: What topic does Ilham discuss on the podcast?
quiz.explanation: The host introduces the topic as sincerity, or ikhlas, with guest Ilham.

quiz.question: How does Ilham define sincerity?
options: Doing something good for Allah's sake alone, not for praise or image
Doing good for a good feeling
quiz.explanation: Ilham defines sincerity as doing something good for Allah's sake alone, not for praise, image, or even a good feeling.

quiz.question: What moment made Ilham notice his habit of posting about good deeds?
options: His first thought after helping a neighbor was that he should post about it
quiz.explanation: After helping an elderly neighbor with groceries, his first thought was that he should post about it.

quiz.question: What did Ilham start doing after that realization?
options: Doing small good things and telling no one, not even close friends
quiz.explanation: He started doing small good things and deliberately telling no one, not even his closest friends.

quiz.question: What advice does Ilham give for people who want recognition for good deeds?
options: Judge yourself harshly until it stops
Notice the urge without judging yourself, and gently choose quiet instead
Give up trying to be sincere
quiz.explanation: He advises noticing the urge without harsh judgment, and gently choosing quiet instead, again and again.

title: A Quiet Confession Between Two Coworkers
script: Dinda: [tense] Reza, can I tell you something, and you promise it stays between us?
Reza: [calm] Of course. You know I don't repeat things, especially not things that matter to you.
Dinda: [nervously] Last month, a colleague told me something very personal about her family, and she asked me not to share it.
Reza: [gently] Okay. You don't have to tell me the details. What's actually worrying you right now?
Dinda: [thoughtful] A few weeks later, another coworker asked me directly if I knew anything about it.
Reza: [curious] What did you say?
Dinda: [honestly] For a second, I almost answered honestly, just to seem interesting, or maybe helpful in that moment.
Reza: [understanding] That's a very human urge, honestly. Gossip feels good for about five seconds.
Dinda: [reflective] I remembered her trust though, and I simply said, that's not mine to share with anyone.
Reza: [warmly] Good for you. How did the coworker react to that?
Dinda: [thoughtful] She seemed a little disappointed, and she even pushed a bit further, asking more questions.
Reza: [encouraging] Did you stay firm?
Dinda: [determined] Yes. I stayed quiet, even though part of me felt awkward saying no twice to the same person.
Reza: [sincere] Some trust is more valuable than a moment of interesting gossip. You made the right call, Dinda.
Dinda: [warmly] Later, my colleague thanked me for something unrelated, without even knowing what had happened at the office that day.
Reza: [thoughtful] Does she know how close her secret came to slipping out?
Dinda: [gently] No, and I don't think she needs to know. That would only make her anxious for no reason.
Reza: [reflective] That's true trustworthiness, I think. Protecting someone quietly, without even needing them to know you protected them.
Dinda: [peacefully] I used to think honesty only meant telling the truth. Now I think it also means knowing when to stay quiet.
Reza: [warmly] That's a wise way to see it. I'm glad you told me, even though I'll forget the details by tomorrow.

quiz.question: What did Dinda's colleague ask her to do?
options: Not share something personal about her family
quiz.explanation: The colleague told Dinda something personal about her family and asked her not to share it.

quiz.question: What did Dinda almost do when another coworker asked about the secret?
options: Answer honestly just to seem interesting or helpful
quiz.explanation: For a second, Dinda almost answered honestly, just to seem interesting or helpful in that moment.

quiz.question: What did Dinda finally say to the coworker?
options: That's not mine to share with anyone
quiz.explanation: Dinda said, that's not mine to share with anyone, remembering her colleague's trust.

quiz.question: Does Dinda's colleague know how close the secret came to slipping out?
options: No, and Dinda doesn't think she needs to know
quiz.explanation: Dinda says her colleague does not know, and she doesn't think she needs to, since it would only cause anxiety.

quiz.question: What does Dinda now believe honesty also means?
quiz.explanation: Dinda concludes that honesty also means knowing when to stay quiet, not only telling the truth.

title: Two Neighbors Compare Notes on Staying Patient
script: Sri: [tired] Amir, honestly, this year has tested my patience more than any year I can remember.
Amir: [gently] I understand that more than you might think. My own year hasn't been easy either.
Sri: [curious] What happened to you? You always seem so calm at the mosque, greeting everyone with that same warm smile.
Amir: [thoughtful] I lost my job in January. I still haven't found steady work since then.
Sri: [surprised] I had no idea. You never once complained about it, not even quietly.
Amir: [reflective] What would complaining actually fix? It only makes the waiting feel heavier for me and everyone around me.
Sri: [touched] That's a strong way to think. I wish I could manage my own stress that calmly.
Amir: [warmly] It isn't calm every single day, believe me. Some nights I lie awake, worried and frustrated about money.
Sri: [gently] What do you do on those nights?
Amir: [sincere] I pray, and I remind myself that this hardship is temporary, even when it doesn't feel that way.
Sri: [thoughtful] I've been struggling with my mother's illness this year, and some days I feel close to breaking completely.
Amir: [warmly] I noticed you visiting the hospital often. I never asked, because I didn't want to intrude on something private.
Sri: [honestly] I appreciate that, actually. Some people ask too many questions, and it becomes exhausting to keep answering them.
Amir: [gently] For what it's worth, I've seen how patiently you handle her appointments, even while working full time.
Sri: [reflective] Some days patience feels impossible. I snap at small things that don't even matter.
Amir: [understanding] That's normal too. Righteousness isn't about never struggling, it's about returning to patience again after we fail at it.
Sri: [thoughtful] I like that. I always thought righteous people simply never got tired or frustrated at all.
Amir: [warmly] No one is like that, honestly. We just keep quietly trying, and trust that the effort itself matters to Allah.
Sri: [peacefully] Talking with you today actually helped more than you probably realize, Amir.
Amir: [gently] It helped me too, Sri. Sometimes we forget everyone around us is carrying something heavy too.

quiz.question: What happened to Amir in January?
quiz.explanation: Amir explains he lost his job in January and still hasn't found steady work.

quiz.question: Why does Amir say complaining doesn't help?
options: It only makes the waiting feel heavier for everyone
It is against his religion to speak
quiz.explanation: Amir says complaining only makes the waiting feel heavier for himself and everyone around him.

quiz.question: What has Sri been struggling with this year?
quiz.explanation: Sri says she has been struggling with her mother's illness this year.

quiz.question: Why did Amir never ask Sri about her hospital visits?
options: He didn't want to intrude on something private
quiz.explanation: Amir noticed her visiting often but never asked because he didn't want to intrude on something private.

quiz.question: According to Amir, what is righteousness really about?
options: Returning to patience again after we fail at it
quiz.explanation: Amir says righteousness isn't about never struggling, it's about returning to patience again after failing at it.

title: My Grandfather's Quiet Habit of Gratitude
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] My grandfather had a small habit that I only truly noticed after many, many years of watching him.
Narrator: [gently] Every single night, right before sleeping, he quietly said thanks for three simple, ordinary things.
Narrator: [curious] Sometimes it was just warm food on the table, or a car that started without trouble, or a short phone call from family.
Narrator: [reflective] I once asked him why he did this small habit so faithfully, every single night without exception.
Narrator: [warmly] He said, a grateful heart rarely stays angry for long, and it rarely stays truly empty either.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I asked if he ever skipped a night, maybe when he was too tired, or too upset about something.
Narrator: [gently] He smiled and said those were exactly the nights he needed the habit most, not the nights he could skip it.
Narrator: [honestly] I did not understand him fully back then. I thought gratitude was something you felt only during good times.
Narrator: [reflective] Years later, during a very difficult season of my own life, I remembered his words almost by accident.
Narrator: [with feeling] I tried it one night, forcing myself to name three small things despite feeling genuinely hopeless about everything else.
Narrator: [softly] It felt strange at first, almost forced, like I was pretending to feel something I clearly did not feel.
Narrator: [with wonder] But slowly, night after night, something shifted quietly inside me, even while my actual circumstances stayed exactly the same.
Narrator: [warmly] After he passed away, I started this same quiet habit myself, and I still continue it faithfully every single night now.
Narrator: [sincere] It's such a small, invisible thing, yet it has slowly changed how I see my whole ordinary day.
Narrator: [reflective] Nobody knows I do this. I've never mentioned it to my friends, and I never plan to, honestly.
Narrator: [peacefully] Righteousness, I have learned, often lives quietly inside these small, honest habits, far from anyone's attention or praise.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandfather do every night before sleeping?
options: He quietly said thanks for three simple things
quiz.explanation: Every night before sleeping, he quietly said thanks for three simple, ordinary things.

quiz.question: According to the grandfather, when did he need the habit most?
options: On tired or upset nights, not nights he could skip it
He didn't need it at all
quiz.explanation: He said the tired or upset nights were exactly the nights he needed the habit most.

quiz.question: When did the narrator finally try the habit herself?
options: Years later, during a very difficult season of her life
quiz.explanation: Years later, during a difficult season of her own life, she remembered his words and tried it.

quiz.question: How did the habit feel for the narrator at first?

quiz.explanation: She says it felt strange at first, almost forced, like pretending to feel something she didn't feel.

quiz.explanation: She says nobody knows she does this, she has never mentioned it to friends, and never plans to.
